result.summary: Niobe, proud of her wealth, lineage and fourteen children, scorns Latona and forbids the Theban women to worship her. Apollo and Diana kill all her children, and Niobe, grieving, turns to weeping stone.

scenes.title: Niobe's pride and Manto's command
scenes.summary: Despite Arachne's fate, Niobe is proud of her children. Manto commands the Theban women to honor Latona, and they obey.
scenes.stakes: Niobe risks divine anger by her pride; the women must honor Latona.

scenes.title: Niobe scorns Latona
scenes.summary: Niobe boasts of her ancestry, wealth and children, belittles Latona's two children, and orders the women to stop the sacrifice.
scenes.stakes: Niobe risks the gods' wrath; the women risk neglecting the goddess.

scenes.title: Latona appeals to her children
scenes.summary: On Mount Cynthus Latona complains to Apollo and Diana, who descend in clouds to Thebes.
scenes.stakes: Latona fears losing her divinity and worship.

scenes.title: The sons are slain
scenes.summary: Apollo shoots the seven sons of Amphion on the plain; Amphion kills himself.

scenes.title: Daughters die, Niobe turns to stone
scenes.summary: Niobe defies Latona, her daughters are shot one by one, and she turns to stone and is carried to her homeland, still weeping.
scenes.stakes: Niobe loses her last child and her own life and form.

notable_quotes.reason: Niobe's desperate plea to spare her youngest daughter.
Closing image of Niobe as weeping marble.

analysis.text: Niobe's hubris leads to total loss, continuing Ovid's pattern of mortals punished for defying gods, as with Arachne.
The tale reflects ancient Greek warnings against excessive pride and comparison with the gods.

legacy.text: Niobe became a lasting emblem of grief; 'Niobe all tears' echoes in Shakespeare's Hamlet.

fun_facts.text: A weeping rock formation on Mount Sipylus in Turkey is traditionally called Niobe.

language_notes.text: "Had known her" means Niobe knew Arachne from girlhood, when both lived in Mæonia (Lydia) and Sipylus, before Niobe married.
Arachne, the Lydian weaver, was turned into a spider for rivaling Minerva; Niobe ignores this warning against defying gods.
Ismenus is the river at Thebes; "women of Ismenus" means the women of Thebes.
Niobe's mother Dione was a sister of the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, so Niobe claims descent from Atlas.
Her husband Amphion built Thebes' walls by playing his lyre, so the stones moved into place by his music.
"In travail" means in labor, giving birth.
Delos was a floating island, hence "unstable place." Latona gave birth there to Apollo and Diana after wandering.
"Am called in question" means her divine status is being doubted or challenged, because Niobe has denied her worship.
The daughter of Tantalus is Niobe, who boasted of her many children and mocked Latona for having only two.
Phœbe is Diana, Phœbus's sister. The citadel of Cadmus is Thebes, which Cadmus founded.
Tyrian dye is the costly purple made at Tyre, a sign of wealth and royal status.
The palæstra was the wrestling ground of Greek athletes, who rubbed their bodies with oil.
Delian God means Apollo, who was born on the island of Delos.
The parenthesis means Ilioneus wrongly prays to all the gods, though two of them are the very ones killing his family.
"Glut" and "satiate" mean to feed to excess; Niobe bitterly tells Latona to gorge herself on her grief.
The twanging bowstring is Diana's, Latona's daughter, shooting the sisters; the text only implies the archer, and the braces mark translator's added words.
"Biers" are the stands on which corpses were laid out before burial; "black array" means mourning dress.
"Husband" refers to Amphion, who in Ovid's account killed himself after his sons' deaths.
"Native land" is Lydia in Asia Minor, where Niobe was born; she is carried there by a whirlwind.

context_notes.text: Manto, a prophetess and daughter of the seer Tiresias, speaks here as Latona's mouthpiece, ordering Thebans to honor Latona and her children, Apollo and Diana.
Tantalus, a son of Jupiter, was admitted to the gods' feasts. He later was punished for abusing that favor.
Niobe's husband Amphion was a son of Jupiter, so Jupiter is her grandfather and also her father-in-law.
Latona (Leto) bore Apollo and Diana to Jupiter. Niobe's boasting led Thebans to abandon Latona's worship, which provokes her anger here.
Juno is queen of the gods and Latona's rival, so Latona yields only to her.
Amphion was Niobe's husband and king of Thebes. His suicide follows the loss of all his sons.
Latona was mother of Apollo and Diana. Niobe had mocked her for having only two children, and they avenged the insult by killing Niobe's children.
The weeping rock on Mount Sipylus in Lydia was pointed out in antiquity as Niobe's petrified form.

literary_notes.text: The remark that she would be happiest "if she had not so seemed to herself" hints that her self-regard will bring ruin.
Her gold-woven robes, tossing hair and haughty glances show her vanity before she speaks.
She sneers that two children are only a seventh of hers; the two will prove deadlier than her fourteen are safe.
Niobe imagines losing only some children and still outnumbering Latona, while the reader knows she will lose all.
Sipylus fleeing the arrow is compared to a pilot spreading sails before a storm, conveying urgent, hopeless flight.
The repeated "together" stresses the brothers' unity in death and heightens the pathos.
Ilioneus prays to all the gods, but the reader knows the gods he addresses are his killers.
Apollo's belated pity, too late to recall the arrow, softens the killing and makes the loss more tragic.
The narrator's opening cry of "Alas!" shows sympathy and sets up a stark contrast between Niobe's former pride and her present ruin.
Niobe claims victory in the midst of total loss, a defiant boast that shows the pride that provoked the punishment.
The mother's plea is cut off by the very death she begs against, which makes the pathos bitterly sudden.
Piled-up details of motionless hair, bloodless color and fixed eyes show the body becoming stone step by step.
The marble that still weeps makes Niobe's grief eternal, a lasting warning against pride toward the gods.
